analysis.one_liner: Requires quarterly public reports to Congress on Medicare and Medicaid fraud investigations and prosecutions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2024 with three Republican sponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services to report to four congressional committees, every three months for two years, on Medicare and Medicaid fraud: how many investigations the office ran, how many criminal prosecutions and civil lawsuits followed, how much money was allegedly stolen in each case, what charges were brought, and how many people and companies were barred from federal health programs. It creates no new enforcement power and no new funding; it only requires regular reporting on work the Inspector General already does.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid, and the public generally, would get a regular, detailed accounting of health care fraud investigations, prosecutions, and the dollar amounts involved. Congressional committees with oversight of these programs would get current data on whether fraud cases are actually being pursued, which could support later legislation or hearings.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the HHS Inspector General to report every three months, for two years, on the number of Medicare and Medicaid fraud investigations, the criminal prosecutions and civil actions that resulted, the dollar amount of fraud alleged in each, the charges filed, and the number of individuals and entities excluded from federal health care programs [S2].
Delivers these reports to the House Ways and Means, House Energy and Commerce, Senate Finance, and Senate HELP committees, the panels that write Medicare and Medicaid law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: No one directly. The bill authorizes no new money and directs the Inspector General to do the reporting with existing funds. The practical cost is staff time at the Inspector General's office to compile quarterly reports, and greater scrutiny for health care companies and individuals defrauding the programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: HHS watchdog staff time; fraud perpetrators face scrutiny

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes no additional funds, so the Inspector General must absorb the reporting workload into existing appropriations; if the office is already stretched, reporting could come at the expense of other work [S2].

The bill only requires reports; it does not change fraud enforcement itself, add investigators, or directly recover any money, so its practical effect depends on Congress or agencies acting on what the reports show [S2].

It creates a duplicate channel of information: the Inspector General already publicly reports fraud enforcement results, so the mandate may add paperwork without producing information the public cannot otherwise get.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: regular, structured data on health care fraud enforcement going to the committees that oversee Medicare and Medicaid. The cost is small and mostly administrative, since no new funding is involved. The honest limitation is that a reporting mandate changes nothing on its own; it is a transparency tool whose value depends on someone using the information.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees in September 2024, then to an Energy and Commerce health subcommittee in December, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025, which kills the bill.

narrative.text: Rep. Aaron Bean of Florida introduced the bill on September 18, 2024, joined by Reps. Rick Allen and Glenn Grothman, both Republicans [S2].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee [S1].
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care providers and companies that bill Medicare and Medicaid, including any engaged in fraudulent billing, are better off: the quarterly public accounting of fraud investigations and prosecutions never materialized, and the committees that oversee the programs never received the data. No one else is measurably worse off, since the bill would only have required reports using existing staff and funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care fraud enforcement stayed out of the spotlight

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican sponsors, so no record shows how the broader House or any committee would have split on it; it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Health care providers and companies billing Medicare and Medicaid
industries.note: Quarterly reports would name the dollar amounts of fraud alleged in prosecutions and civil actions and the number of individuals and entities barred from federal health programs, putting a recurring spotlight on billing fraud. The industry interest in avoiding that public accounting runs against the interest of taxpayers who fund the programs.
The watchdog office would gain a recurring statutory mandate and visibility for its fraud work, but must produce the reports with existing funds and no new appropriation.
